Payroll in Colombia: why the real cost is far more than the salary

Social security, payroll levies and statutory benefits. What's paid on top of the salary, what to provision, and why an all-inclusive salary isn't always the right call.

An employee's cost has three layers

Colombia is probably the country in the region where salary and real cost diverge most. Anyone budgeting on the wage falls short systematically, because there are three distinct layers on top:

  • Social security. Health, pension and occupational risk. Part is deducted from the employee's pay and part is contributed by the company. Occupational risk depends on the activity: it isn't the same for an office as for a building site.
  • Payroll levies. Contributions to training, family welfare and the compensation fund. They fall entirely on the company and there are exemptions depending on the salary level.
  • Statutory benefits. The service bonus, severance savings with their interest, and holidays. They aren't paid with the monthly payroll: they accrue and are paid on specific dates.

Statutory benefits are why a Colombian company can have a balanced year and still run out of cash in June and December: those months concentrate payments that built up all year.

Severance savings: the mechanism most misunderstood

Severance savings aren't paid to the employee monthly and don't stay with the company. They accrue through the year and are deposited into a fund on the due date. They also earn annual interest for the employee, which is paid directly.

The errors we see:

  • Not provisioning month by month, and discovering the full amount right before the deposit date.
  • Calculating the interest on the wrong balance, or over the wrong period.
  • Not allowing for authorised partial withdrawals, which change the balance.
  • Forgetting that an employee who joined mid-year has a pro-rata base, not a full one.

The transport allowance and each item's base

A small detail that throws many payrolls out: the transport allowance is paid below a certain salary level, and it counts towards the base of some things and not others. Putting it where it doesn't belong, or leaving it out where it does, changes benefits and contributions at once.

The general principle applies everywhere: every pay item has to be classified once — whether it contributes, whether it's a benefits base, whether it's salary or not — and the calculation inherits it. Classifying it on every payslip guarantees that one month it'll be done differently.

An all-inclusive salary isn't automatically better

Above a certain salary level you can agree an all-inclusive salary, which folds the statutory benefits into the salary itself. It simplifies payroll a lot, which is why it's often proposed as a solution.

But it isn't always the right call, and the decision isn't a payroll one: it's about cost and negotiation. What is certain is that it has a legal minimum and rules of its own, and applying it wrongly leaves the company exposed.

On top comes electronic payroll, which has to be transmitted on its own schedule. It feeds off the calculation: if the calculation is misclassified, so is the filing. We cover it alongside e-invoicing and the DIAN.

Rates, caps, exemption thresholds and the all-inclusive salary minimum are updated every year. Confirm the current figures with your employment adviser: what's explained here is the mechanism.
